scenes.visual: COLOR MAP (both films, and match the figure dna-ladder-parts.webp if its base colours differ, then keep them identical in both films): old strands and their backbones GREY, new strands GOLD, base A RED, base T BLUE, base C GREEN, base G PURPLE, labels WHITE on dark navy. Every strand is drawn as a backbone with an ARROWHEAD at one end. Bases are labelled rectangular blocks with their letter; no molecular structures. Title card: One Strand Is Enough. A short grey ladder segment fades in under the title and gently rotates.

scenes.tts: Suppose I tore a D N A molecule down the middle and threw one half away. Could you rebuild the half I threw away, letter for letter? By the end of this film, you can.
scenes.caption: Suppose I tore a DNA molecule down the middle and threw one half away. Could you rebuild the half I threw away, letter for letter? By the end of this film, you can.
scenes.visual: A straight grey ladder of six rungs, coloured base blocks meeting in the middle. A pair of cartoon hands rips it lengthwise; the lower half slides off screen into a bin. The upper half stays, bases pointing down. A large question mark pulses over the empty space where the lower half was.
scenes.narration: Suppose I tore a DNA molecule down the middle and threw one half away. Could you rebuild the half I threw away, letter for letter? By the end of this film, you can.

scenes.tts: Start with one building block, a nucleotide. It has three parts: a sugar called deoxyribose, a phosphate group, and a base. The base carries the information. D N A uses four bases: adenine, thymine, cytosine and guanine. We write them A, T, C and G.
scenes.caption: Start with one building block, a nucleotide. It has three parts: a sugar called deoxyribose, a phosphate group, and a base. The base carries the information. DNA uses four bases: adenine, thymine, cytosine and guanine. We write them A, T, C and G.
scenes.visual: Clear the frame. Three pieces fly in and snap together as each is named: a rounded pentagon-shaped block labelled sugar (deoxyribose), a small circle labelled phosphate, a rectangle labelled base. Label the assembled unit NUCLEOTIDE. Then four copies appear in a row, their base blocks recolouring to RED A, BLUE T, GREEN C, PURPLE G, each with its full name underneath.
scenes.narration: Start with one building block, a nucleotide. It has three parts: a sugar called deoxyribose, a phosphate group, and a base. The base carries the information. DNA uses four bases: adenine, thymine, cytosine and guanine. We write them A, T, C and G.

scenes.tts: Nucleotides join into a chain called a strand. The sugar of one nucleotide bonds to the phosphate of the next. That is a covalent bond, a strong bond in which atoms share electrons. The bases stick out to one side.
scenes.visual: The four nucleotides slide together vertically. Each sugar-to-phosphate link flashes white with the label covalent bond. The joined sugars and phosphates become a continuous grey backbone; the base blocks all point right. An ARROWHEAD grows at the bottom end of the backbone. A counter in the top corner appears: strands 1.
scenes.narration: Nucleotides join into a chain called a strand. The sugar of one nucleotide bonds to the phosphate of the next. That is a covalent bond, a strong bond in which atoms share electrons. The bases stick out to one side.

scenes.tts: Now a second strand lines up, bases facing bases. Weak attractions called hydrogen bonds hold each facing pair together. But only two kinds of pair fit well. A fits with T. C fits with G.
scenes.visual: A second grey strand slides in from the right with its bases pointing left; its ARROWHEAD points UP, opposite to the first strand. As facing bases meet, short dashed white lines appear between them labelled hydrogen bonds. RED A and BLUE T blocks have matching notched edges and click shut; GREEN C and PURPLE G likewise. Counter: strands 2.
scenes.narration: Now a second strand lines up, bases facing bases. Weak attractions called hydrogen bonds hold each facing pair together. But only two kinds of pair fit well. A fits with T. C fits with G.

scenes.tts: Watch what happens when A meets C. Their edges do not match, so they fit badly. That is the base-pairing rule. A always pairs with T, and C always pairs with G.
scenes.visual: Zoom on one rung. A RED A block approaches a GREEN C block; their notched edges clash and leave a gap, and the C slides back out with a small red X. A BLUE T slides in instead and clicks. Then a PURPLE G clicks with a GREEN C below it. A rule banner settles at the bottom: A with T, C with G.
scenes.narration: Watch what happens when A meets C. Their edges do not match, so they fit badly. That is the base-pairing rule. A always pairs with T, and C always pairs with G.

scenes.tts: Notice the two arrowheads. Each strand has a direction, and the two strands point opposite ways. Finally the ladder twists along its length into a double helix. The backbones are the sides, and the base pairs are the rungs.
scenes.visual: Zoom out. The two ARROWHEADS pulse, one pointing down, one pointing up. The flat ladder twists smoothly into a schematic double helix, labels sides and rungs appear, then it untwists back to a flat ladder for the next scene. Label the helix schematic.
scenes.narration: Notice the two arrowheads. Each strand has a direction, and the two strands point opposite ways. Finally the ladder twists along its length into a double helix. The backbones are the sides, and the base pairs are the rungs.

scenes.tts: Here is one strand on its own. It reads G, A, T, T, C, A. Before I fill in its partner, write the partner strand yourself.
scenes.visual: One grey strand alone, six base blocks in a column reading G A T T C A in their colours. Six empty dashed slots sit opposite them. A small pencil icon appears beside the slots.
scenes.narration: Here is one strand on its own. It reads G, A, T, T, C, A. Before I fill in its partner, write the partner strand yourself.

scenes.visual: Hold the single strand and the six empty slots. The pencil icon taps gently. Do not fill any slot.

scenes.tts: Across from G goes C. Across from A goes T. So the partner reads C, T, A, A, G, T. Not one letter was a choice. One strand fixed every letter of the other.
scenes.visual: The slots fill one at a time from the top, each block clicking into place in its colour: C T A A G T. When all six are filled, a white bracket spans the pair with the label: one strand fixes its partner.
scenes.narration: Across from G goes C. Across from A goes T. So the partner reads C, T, A, A, G, T. Not one letter was a choice. One strand fixed every letter of the other.

scenes.tts: So here is how a cell copies D N A. Enzymes unzip the helix, and each old strand becomes a template. A template is a pattern that sets the order of a new strand.
scenes.caption: So here is how a cell copies DNA. Enzymes unzip the helix, and each old strand becomes a template. A template is a pattern that sets the order of a new strand.
scenes.visual: Return to a longer grey ladder, about ten rungs. A simple wedge shape labelled enzyme slides down the middle; the two grey strands peel apart into two separate columns. Each old strand gets the label template. Do not show which bonds break.
scenes.narration: So here is how a cell copies DNA. Enzymes unzip the helix, and each old strand becomes a template. A template is a pattern that sets the order of a new strand.

scenes.tts: New nucleotides line up on each template, each one matching the base it faces. When copying ends, there are two molecules. Each has one old grey strand and one new gold strand. Both carry the same base order as the original.
scenes.visual: GOLD backbones with coloured base blocks build down beside each GREY template, one block at a time, following the pairing rule. The two finished molecules drift apart side by side, each GREY plus GOLD. Counter updates: molecules 2, each 1 old plus 1 new. A check mark flashes as the two base orders are compared rung by rung.
scenes.narration: New nucleotides line up on each template, each one matching the base it faces. When copying ends, there are two molecules. Each has one old grey strand and one new gold strand. Both carry the same base order as the original.

scenes.tts: So pairing tells the cell what goes where. Because A pairs only with T, and C only with G, each strand fixes its partner. Pairing does not yet explain how the cell gets almost every letter right.
scenes.visual: The two molecules shrink to the top of the frame. The rule banner A with T, C with G grows to centre, then rewrites as: each strand fixes its partner. A small grey question mark appears beside the word accuracy at the bottom, then fades before the end card.
scenes.narration: So pairing tells the cell what goes where. Because A pairs only with T, and C only with G, each strand fixes its partner. Pairing does not yet explain how the cell gets almost every letter right.

scenes.visual: Clear the frame. End card with one centered line only, no title and no second line: 'Each strand fixes its partner, so either can restore the whole molecule.'
